presentingComplaint: Increasing bloody diarrhoea, up to 9 stools/day with urgency and tenesmus, on day 4 after elective right total hip replacement.
history: 71-year-old woman with a 14-year history of ulcerative colitis (left-sided, previously well controlled on oral mesalazine 2.4 g/day) admitted electively for right total hip arthroplasty for osteoarthritis. Post-operative recovery complicated by escalating loose, bloody stools from post-op day 2, now 8-9 times daily with nocturnal motions, urgency, tenesmus, cramping lower abdominal pain and 3 kg weight loss over the admission. Her mesalazine was inadvertently omitted on the peri-operative drug chart while nil-by-mouth. Regular medications include amlodipine, atorvastatin, levothyroxine, omeprazole and, since surgery, regular diclofenac and codeine for analgesia plus subcutaneous enoxaparin thromboprophylaxis. No recent antibiotics before admission, no foreign travel, no sick contacts. Reports fatigue and anorexia; no vomiting.
examination: Elderly woman, mildly distressed and pale. Dry mucous membranes with reduced skin turgor. Abdomen soft but diffusely tender in the lower quadrants with mild distension and active bowel sounds; no guarding, rigidity or rebound; no palpable mass. Digital rectal examination shows fresh blood and mucus. Surgical hip wound clean and dry. No peripheral oedema; peripheral pulses intact.
imaging: Abdominal X-ray: continuous mucosal oedema/thumbprinting through the descending and sigmoid colon; transverse colonic diameter 4.2 cm (no toxic megacolon, no free air). Flexible sigmoidoscopy (unprepped, limited): continuous, circumferential erythema, loss of vascular pattern, granularity and superficial ulceration with contact bleeding from rectum to descending colon (Mayo endoscopic subscore 3); biopsies taken.
microbiology: Stool C. difficile GDH/toxin and PCR negative; routine stool culture and ova/parasites negative; CMV immunohistochemistry on biopsy pending. Blood cultures not indicated (afebrile, no sepsis).
differentialDiagnoses: Acute severe flare of ulcerative colitis (Truelove-Witts criteria)
Clostridioides difficile infection superimposed on IBD
Ischaemic colitis in an elderly vasculopath
finalDiagnosis: Acute flare of ulcerative colitis (acute severe colitis) precipitated by peri-operative mesalazine omission and NSAID exposure, with negative C. difficile and stool studies.
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e - Inflammatory Bowel Disease
stewardship: Non-infective diagnosis: no antibiotics indicated. C. difficile and stool cultures are negative, so empiric antimicrobials are not warranted and would represent inappropriate use. Management is anti-inflammatory: reinstate/escalate to IV corticosteroids (hydrocortisone 100 mg QDS) for acute severe UC, with day-3 reassessment for rescue therapy (infliximab or ciclosporin) if non-responding. Stop NSAIDs (diclofenac) as a colitis precipitant, review opioid/anticholinergic burden given megacolon risk, correct hypokalaemia and dehydration, continue VTE prophylaxis, and involve colorectal surgery and IBD MDT.
contraindications: Avoid antimotility/opioid agents (codeine, loperamide) in acute severe colitis - risk of toxic megacolon
Withhold empiric antibiotics without evidence of infection
Caution with high-dose corticosteroids in an elderly diabetic-risk peri-operative patient (glycaemia, wound healing)
edgeCases: Peri-operative mesalazine omission on the drug chart is an easily missed medication-reconciliation trigger for the flare
Superimposed C. difficile or CMV colitis can mimic or drive a refractory flare and must be excluded before escalating immunosuppression
Toxic megacolon (transverse colon >6 cm) can supervene rapidly - serial exams and abdominal films needed
Polypharmacy (NSAID + opioid) both worsens colitis and masks/adds abdominal signs in the elderly
expectedMaiK: Recognise acute severe ulcerative colitis flare (Truelove-Witts), exclude C. difficile/infective colitis, stop NSAIDs and antimotility agents, and start IV corticosteroids with day-3 rescue-therapy planning.
